SUBJECT: Douglas "Dougie" Reid, 86
INTERVIEWER: Iain (son)
ALSO PRESENT: Moira (Dougie's wife, Iain's mother) — interjects throughout
SETTING: Living room, Peterhead, Scotland. Television on in the background. Session 1.
PROFILE NOTES: Born 1940. Inshore and deep-sea fisherman for 40 years. Doesn't talk much about the past. Some word-finding difficulty. Lost friends at sea.

Q: Dad, tell me about your first boat.

A: Och. The first boat. [pause] It was a boat, Iain. What d'you want me to say.

Q: Well — what was she called?

A: The... ach. The — it's on the tip of my — Moira, what was the — [Moira: The Morning Star.] No. No, that was Sandy's boat. Ours was the... [pause] It'll come to me.

Q: What was a normal day like?

A: Up at three. Out. Back. Same as anybody.

Q: Come on, Dad. What did it smell like down below?

A: Smell? [laughs] Diesel and wet wool and fish. And Erchie's pipe. Erchie smoked this terrible — black stuff, black twist, you'd cut it off the block with a knife. You'd come home and your mother'd — Moira'd say, you smell like Erchie. [Moira: You did.] Aye. Every time.

Q: Was it dangerous?

A: Ach, everybody asks that. It's the sea. You don't think about it. You just get on.

Q: Mum says there was one winter you didn't go out.

A: [pause, approx. 8 seconds] I had the flu. That's all. I had the flu and the... the boat went out without me. The Ocean — [inaudible] — five of them. Erchie was — [pause] Turn that off, Moira. The television. [sound of TV switching off] [pause] I was in my bed. That's all there is.

Q: I didn't know Erchie was on that boat.

A: Well. [pause] Now you do.

Q: Can you tell me how you met Mum?

A: [Moira: He tells everybody it was the Fisherman's Ball and it wasn't, it was the bus.] It was the Ball. [Moira: It was the bus to Aberdeen, Douglas.] [pause] Well. She'd a red coat on. Whichever it was. A red coat, with the big buttons. That's what I mind.

Q: Do you miss the fishing?

A: Miss it. [pause] I go down the harbour. Most days. There's nothing there now. It's all — what d'you call them. The — for the wind. The wind — the boats that go out to the — service boats. That's all it is now. Nobody I know.

Q: Is there anything you'd want the grandkids to know?

A: Ach, I don't know. Work hard. Be good to your mother. [pause] That's it. Is that enough? I'm tired, son.
